section: Rating data preparation and descriptive summary
text:
Rating data preparation and descriptive summary


Code
question_labels <- c(
  A301 = "Helpful for comparison",
  A302 = "Helpful for detection and integration",
  A303 = "Would use in publication or presentation",
  A304 = "Aesthetically appealing"
)

# All four questions presented the visualization types in the same order.
# The A304 columns retain that order in the export, but their suffixes are
# nonsequential (01, 06, 02, 03, 04, 05, 07).
rating_columns <- list(
  A301 = sprintf("A301_%02d", seq_along(vistypes)),
  A302 = sprintf("A302_%02d", seq_along(vistypes)),
  A303 = sprintf("A303_%02d", seq_along(vistypes)),
  A304 = c(
    "A304_01", "A304_06", "A304_02", "A304_03",
    "A304_04", "A304_05", "A304_07"
  )
)

rating_key <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  rating_columns,
  \(columns, question_code) tibble(
    question_code = question_code,
    rating_column = columns,
    vistype = vistypes
  )
)




Validation checks
if (!identical(names(rating_columns), names(question_labels)) ||
    any(lengths(rating_columns) != length(vistypes)) ||
    anyDuplicated(rating_key$rating_column) ||
    nrow(rating_key) != 28L) {
  stop("The subjective-rating key must contain 28 unique survey columns.")
}

# Validate the explicit key against the question labels embedded in the first
# row of the LimeSurvey export. Stop rather than silently relabel results if the
# questionnaire changes in a future export.
rating_key_validation <- rating_key %>%
  mutate(
    survey_label = as.character(
      unlist(legend[1, rating_column], use.names = FALSE)
    ),
    label_matches = stringr::str_detect(
      survey_label,
      stringr::fixed(vistype)
    )
  )

if (any(is.na(rating_key_validation$survey_label)) ||
    any(!rating_key_validation$label_matches)) {
  stop("The subjective-rating key does not match the embedded survey labels.")
}




Code
likert <- data %>%
  select(ID, all_of(rating_key$rating_column)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    -ID,
    names_to = "rating_column",
    values_to = "rating_raw"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    rating_key %>% select(rating_column, question_code, vistype),
    by = "rating_column"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    vistype = factor(
      vistype,
      levels = vistypes
    ),

    question = factor(
      question_code,
      levels = names(question_labels),
      labels = unname(question_labels)
    ),

    rating = as.integer(
      stringr::str_extract(as.character(rating_raw), "^-?\\d+")
    ),

    rating = if_else(
      rating %in% 1:5,
      rating,
      NA_integer_
    )
  ) %>%
  select(ID, question, vistype, rating)

Ordinal mixed-effects models


Code
likert_model_data <- likert |>
  filter(!is.na(rating)) |>
  mutate(
    ID = factor(ID),
    vistype = droplevels(factor(vistype)),
    rating_ord = ordered(rating, levels = 1:5)
  )

likert_models <- likert_model_data |>
  (\(data) split(data, data$question))() |>
  map(
    \(data_question) clmm(
      rating_ord ~ vistype + (1 | ID),
      data = data_question,
      Hess = TRUE
    )
  )

likert_estimates <- imap_dfr(
  likert_models,
  function(model, question_name) {

    emmeans(
      model,
      ~ vistype,
      mode = "mean.class"
    ) |>
      confint() |>
      as.data.frame() |>
      transmute(
        question = question_name,
        vistype,
        estimated_rating = mean.class,
        lower_ci = asymp.LCL,
        upper_ci = asymp.UCL
      )
  }
)

Model: Separate cumulative-link mixed models with logit link are fitted for each evaluation criterion: rating_ord ~ vistype + (1 | ID). Estimated marginal means use mode = "mean.class": they are model-smoothed mean ratings on the 1–5 scale, with asymptotic pointwise 95% confidence intervals (not adjusted for multiplicity).




Model checks and sensitivity analyses


Code
# 1. Proportional odds: fixed-effects clm with and without visualization-specific
#    thresholds (nominal effects), compared by likelihood-ratio test.
po_tests <- likert_model_data |>
  (\(data) split(data, data$question))() |>
  imap_dfr(function(data_question, question_name) {
    po_fit <- clm(rating_ord ~ vistype, data = data_question)
    npo_fit <- clm(rating_ord ~ 1, nominal = ~ vistype, data = data_question)
    lrt <- anova(po_fit, npo_fit)
    tibble(
      question = question_name,
      lr_statistic = lrt$LR.stat[2],
      df = lrt$df[2],
      p_value = lrt$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
    )
  })

# 2. Model-smoothed vs raw means.
raw_vs_model <- likert |>
  group_by(question, vistype) |>
  summarise(raw_mean = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(question = as.character(question), vistype = as.character(vistype)) |>
  inner_join(
    likert_estimates |> mutate(vistype = as.character(vistype)),
    by = c("question", "vistype")
  ) |>
  mutate(abs_difference = abs(estimated_rating - raw_mean))
max_raw_model_difference <- max(raw_vs_model$abs_difference)

# 3. Linear mixed model on the 1–5 ratings: same Dunnett contrasts vs Basic.
likert_lmm_contrasts <- likert_model_data |>
  (\(data) split(data, data$question))() |>
  imap_dfr(function(data_question, question_name) {
    fit <- lmer(rating ~ vistype + (1 | ID), data = data_question)
    question_emmeans <- emmeans(fit, ~ vistype)
    set.seed(20261118)  # adjust = "mvt" integrates numerically (Monte Carlo)
    contrast(
      question_emmeans,
      method = "trt.vs.ctrl",
      ref = which(question_emmeans@levels$vistype == "basic"),
      adjust = "mvt"
    ) |>
      confint() |>
      as.data.frame() |>
      transmute(
        question = question_name,
        vistype = stringr::str_remove(contrast, " - basic$"),
        lmm_difference = estimate,
        lmm_lower = lower.CL,
        lmm_upper = upper.CL
      )
  })

po_tests |>
  mutate(p_value = format_p_value(p_value)) |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    digits = 1,
    col.names = c("Evaluation criterion", "LR statistic", "df", "p"),
    caption = paste(
      "Proportional-odds check: fixed-effects cumulative-link model vs a model with",
      "visualization-specific thresholds (likelihood-ratio test)"
    ),
    table.attr = kable_table_attributes
  )

Proportional odds. The likelihood-ratio test rejects proportional odds for 4 of 4 criteria (p from < .001 to .007): the visualizations differ in how ratings are spread over the scale, not only in their location. The analysis therefore reports model-smoothed mean ratings, which stay close to the raw means (largest absolute difference 0.08 scale points), rather than interpreting the odds ratios.
Random-effects structure. Each participant gave exactly one rating per visualization and criterion. Participant-specific visualization effects ((1 + vistype | ID)) would have one observation per random effect and are not identifiable separately from the observation-level latent error, so the random intercept is the maximal identifiable structure. The linear mixed model below is a sensitivity check that does not rely on proportional odds.

question_columns <- unname(question_labels)

likert_vistype_order <- c(
  "basic",
  "adjacent",
  "triple_CI",
  "uncert_markers",
  "animation",
  "bivariate_range",
  "bivariate_corner"
)

likert_display_labels <- c(
  basic = "Basic topoplot",
  adjacent = "Adjacent plots",
  triple_CI = "Confidence intervals",
  uncert_markers = "Uncertainty markers",
  animation = "Animation",
  bivariate_range = "Bivariate range",
  bivariate_corner = "Bivariate corner"
)

likert_panel_titles <- c(
  "Helpful for comparison" = "Helpful for comparison",
  "Helpful for detection and integration" = "Helpful for detection & integration",
  "Would use in publication or presentation" = "Would use in publication",
  "Aesthetically appealing" = "Aesthetically appealing"
)

make_likert_estimate_plot <- function(
  question_name,
  show_x = TRUE,
  show_labels = TRUE
) {

  plot_data <- likert_estimates |>
    filter(question == question_name) |>
    mutate(
      colour_group = if_else(vistype == "basic", "basic", "other"),
    
      display_label = unname(
        likert_display_labels[as.character(vistype)]
      ),
    
      vistype = factor(
        vistype,
        levels = rev(likert_vistype_order)
      )
    )

  p <- ggplot(
    plot_data,
      aes(
    x = estimated_rating,
    y = vistype,
    colour = colour_group
  )
  ) +
    geom_errorbar(
      aes(
        xmin = lower_ci,
        xmax = upper_ci
      ),
      orientation = "y",
      width = 0.12,
      linewidth = 0.55
    ) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +

    # Estimated values
    geom_text(
      aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", estimated_rating)),
      nudge_y = 0.32,
      vjust = 0.5,
      size = 30 / ggplot2::.pt
    ) +

    scale_colour_manual(
  values = c(
    basic = "#3B78B4",
    other = "#222222"
  ),
  guide = "none"
) +

    scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = 1:5,
      labels = function(x) sprintf("%.0f", x),
      expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02))
    ) +

    # Hide ordinary y-axis labels
    scale_y_discrete(
      labels = NULL,
      expand = expansion(add = 0.5)
    ) +

    # Show custom labels placed slightly outside the panel
    coord_cartesian(
      xlim = c(1, 5),
      clip = "off"
    ) +

    labs(
      title = unname(likert_panel_titles[question_name]),
      x = NULL,
      y = NULL
    ) +

    theme_classic(base_family = "Lato", base_size = 20) +

    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(
        hjust = 0.5,
        face = "bold",
        size = 50
      ),
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 20),
      axis.title.x = element_text(size = 20),
      axis.text.y = element_blank(),
      axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
      axis.line.y = element_blank(),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),

      # Space for custom labels
       plot.margin = margin(
    t = 5.5,
    r = 5.5,
        b = 8,
    l = if (show_labels) 245 else 12
  )
    )

  if (show_labels) {
    p <- p +
      geom_text(
        data = plot_data,
        aes(
          x = 0.9,
          y = vistype,
          label = display_label,
          colour = colour_group
        ),
        inherit.aes = FALSE,
        hjust = 1,
        size = 14,
        lineheight = 1
      )
  }

  if (!show_x) {
    p <- p +
      theme(
        axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank()
      )
  }

  p
}

p2 <- make_likert_estimate_plot(

        margin = margin(t = 10, b = 6)

title: Task 2: hit or miss
text: The Task 2 page scores each response on a continuous 0–1 scale. This page asks a simpler question: did participants click the peak region, a region right next to it, or somewhere else?

title: Task 2: hit or miss
text:
Definitions

Hit — the selected region is the peak (region score = 1). For one stimulus two regions are tied at 1.00, and either counts.
Near hit — the selected region shares a border with the peak region. Regions have 3–8 neighbours (mean 5.2); touching only at a corner does not count.
Miss — any other region.
A random click would give 1.6% hits and 6.3% near hits.

title: Task 2: hit or miss

    `Hit or near hit` = mean(close == 1),

title: Task 2: hit or miss
text:
Models
Two logistic mixed models with the predictors of the Task 2 models, vistype + pattern + position_c + (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus) + (1 | stimulus:vistype): one for an exact hit, one for a hit or near hit. The last term gives each of the 210 images (stimulus × visualization) its own intercept, because the ~15 responses to one image are not independent.


Code
hit_miss_models <- list(
  `Hit` = glmmTMB(
    hit ~ vistype + pattern + position_c +
      (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus) + (1 | stimulus:vistype),
    family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = hit_miss
  ),
  `Hit or near hit` = glmmTMB(
    close ~ vistype + pattern + position_c +
      (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus) + (1 | stimulus:vistype),
    family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = hit_miss
  )
)

# Overall test of visualization type: likelihood-ratio test against the same
# model without vistype.
hit_miss_overall <- purrr::imap_dfr(hit_miss_models, \(model, name) {
  reduced <- update(model, . ~ . - vistype)
  chi <- as.numeric(2 * (logLik(model) - logLik(reduced)))
  df <- attr(logLik(model), "df") - attr(logLik(reduced), "df")
  tibble(outcome = name, chi = chi, df = df, p = pchisq(chi, df, lower.tail = FALSE))
})
overall_text <- function(name) {
  r <- hit_miss_overall[hit_miss_overall$outcome == name, ]
  sprintf("χ²(%d) = %.1f, p = %.2f", r$df, r$chi, r$p)
}

stopifnot(all(purrr::map_lgl(hit_miss_models, \(m) {
  m$fit$convergence == 0 && isTRUE(m$sdr$pdHess)
})))

hit_miss_estimates <- purrr::imap_dfr(hit_miss_models, \(model, name) {
  emmeans(model, ~vistype, type = "response") |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    transmute(outcome = name, vistype, prob, lower = asymp.LCL, upper = asymp.UCL)
})

hit_miss_contrasts <- purrr::imap_dfr(hit_miss_models, \(model, name) {
  emmeans(model, ~vistype) |>
    contrast(method = "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = "basic", adjust = "none") |>
    summary(infer = TRUE, type = "response") |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    transmute(
      outcome = name,
      vistype = stringr::str_remove(contrast, " / basic$"),
      odds.ratio, lower = asymp.LCL, upper = asymp.UCL, p.value
    )
})

hit_miss_estimates |>
  mutate(
    vistype = factor(vistype, levels = levels(hit_miss$vistype)),
    value = sprintf("%.0f%% [%.0f, %.0f]", 100 * prob, 100 * lower, 100 * upper)
  ) |>
  select(outcome, vistype, value) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = value) |>
  left_join(
    hit_miss_contrasts |>
      transmute(
        outcome = paste(outcome, "p"),
        vistype = factor(vistype, levels = levels(hit_miss$vistype)),
        p = format_pvalue_html(p.value)
      ) |>
      tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = p),
    by = "vistype"
  ) |>
  arrange(vistype) |>
  mutate(
    vistype = table_vistype(vistype),
    across(ends_with(" p"), \(x) tidyr::replace_na(x, "reference"))
  ) |>
  select(vistype, `Hit`, `Hit p`, `Hit or near hit`, `Hit or near hit p`) |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    escape = FALSE,
    col.names = c("Visualization", "Hit [95% CI]", "p vs Basic",

title: Task 2: hit or miss
text:
Takeaways

Exact hits are rare for every visualization (15%–21%), but well above chance (1.6%). Adjacent plots has the most exact hits.
Counting near hits changes the ranking: Uncertainty markers lands on or next to the peak most often (49%), and Basic topoplot least often (38%).
Once each image gets its own intercept, the overall effect of visualization type is not statistically significant for either outcome (hit χ²(6) = 8.5, p = 0.21; hit or near hit χ²(6) = 9.3, p = 0.16).
The stimulus matters more than the visualization: hit rates range from 0% to 70% across the 30 stimuli.

title: Task 1
text:
Task 1 examined whether adding uncertainty information made the underlying spatial pattern in an EEG topoplot more difficult to recognize. On each trial, participants saw a target ERP pattern and two alternative topoplots. They selected the alternative that most closely matched the target. One alternative represented the same ERP-pattern class as the target, while the other represented a different class.
The task included three characteristic ERP patterns: MMN, P3, and N170. Each was shown using each of the seven visualization types. This produced 21 trials per participant, each on separate page. Trial order was randomized separately for every participant.






Figure 1: Example comparison trial. Participants selected the alternative whose spatial pattern most closely matched the target.

title: Task 1
text:
Trial reconstruction and presentation order

Trial information was reconstructed from the survey records and joined with each participant’s responses using participant, trial, and question identifiers.



Code
# Task 1 trial reconstruction, shared by pages/task1.qmd and pages/time.qmd.
# Requires `data` and `get_field()` from scripts/analysis_setup.R.

task1_order <- data %>%
  dplyr::select(ID, A125_02) %>%
  tidyr::separate_rows(A125_02, sep = "\n") %>%
  dplyr::filter(A125_02 != "") %>%
  dplyr::transmute(
    ID,
    position = as.integer(get_field(A125_02, "position")),
    trial    = as.integer(get_field(A125_02, "trial")),
    question = get_field(A125_02, "question"),
    stimulus = get_field(A125_02, "stimulus"),
    expected = as.integer(get_field(A125_02, "expected")),
    answered = as.integer(get_field(A125_02, "answered")),
    correct  = as.integer(get_field(A125_02, "correct"))
  ) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(ID, position)

task1_design <- data %>%
  dplyr::select(ID, A124_01) %>%
  tidyr::separate_rows(A124_01, sep = "\n") %>%
  dplyr::filter(A124_01 != "") %>%
  dplyr::transmute(

title: Task 1
text:
Accuracy analysis

Every response was coded as correct (1) or incorrect (0).
The analysis contains 3,129 responses: 149 participants × 21 trials.
Visualization type was treated as a categorical variable, with the basic topoplot as the reference condition.
Presentation position was represented by the centered variable position_c, calculated as position - mean(position). Because positions ranged from 1 to 21, their mean was 11. Thus, position_c = 0 represents position 11, negative values represent earlier trials, and positive values represent later trials. This variable tests whether accuracy changed linearly as participants progressed through the task.
No responses were excluded for missing values. All 3,129 reconstructed records contained accuracy, visualization type, ERP pattern, presentation position, target stimulus, and distractor stimulus.

Population-average accuracy

A logistic mixed-effects model estimated the probability of a correct response:
correct ~ vistype + pattern + position_c +
  (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus) + (1 | wrong_image)
Some participants were generally more accurate than others. Because every participant completed 21 trials, we added a participant random intercept, which allows each participant to have their own baseline accuracy. The model then examines whether accuracy changed with visualization type or trial position across participants.
ERP pattern was included as a fixed effect, so visualization comparisons account for systematic accuracy differences among MMN, N170, and P3 trials.
Target and distractor stimuli were included as separate random intercepts. This gives each image its own baseline difficulty in each role and prevents unusually easy or difficult images from being mistaken for visualization effects.
These probabilities are model-based estimates of average accuracy for each visualisation type. Estimates were calculated for the midpoint of the experiment, weighted equally across the three ERP patterns, and averaged over participant and stimulus differences (random effects).







NoteChoosing how to summarize predicted accuracy





There are three ways to summarize the model:








Option
Calculation
What it describes




1
Set participant and stimulus differences to zero.
Average-baseline participants and stimuli.


2
Average over the participants and stimuli observed in the study, using their fitted random effects.
Sample-averaged model prediction.


3
Average over the modelled distributions of participant and stimulus random effects.
Population-averaged model prediction.



We chose option 3 becausewe are more interested in accuracy over population (Hu et al., 1998; Hedeker et al., 2018).
Accuracy-averaging sensitivity check. We compared Options 2 and 3. Across visualisation types, the largest difference was 0.4 percentage points. This difference did not meaningfully change the relative performance of the visualisation types.
This does not make the sample representative of all EEG researchers.









NoteWhy participant-specific random slopes were not retained





We tested whether the effect of trial position differed between participants by adding a participant-specific position slope: (1 + position_c | ID), while retaining the ERP pattern and stimulus terms. The model produced a singular fit and could not estimate this additional variation:

The estimated variance of the position slopes was 0.00047.
The estimated correlation between the baseline accuracy and position slopes was -1.00.

Together, these boundary estimates indicate that the data did not contain enough information to estimate participant baseline differences and participant-specific position effects separately.
We also considered participant-specific effects for visualization type. However, each participant provided only three responses for each visualization. Modeling the seven-level visualization factor would require six additional slopes and their covariances, which the available responses could not support reliably.
We therefore retained the simpler random-intercept model. This does not show that the position and visualization effects are identical for every participant. It means only that these data cannot reliably estimate how those effects differ between participants.

Accuracy differences relative to Basic topoplot

These comparisons estimate the population-average accuracy difference between each visualization and the basic topoplot. They are the primary comparisons for Task 1.
Multiplicity. The six comparisons with Basic form one family. Their intervals are simultaneous 95% confidence intervals with a Dunnett-type (max-|z|) adjustment: the critical value is the 95th percentile of the largest absolute standardized deviation across the six contrasts in the 10,000 simulated coefficient sets. The adjusted p values use the same distribution. An interval that crosses zero means that the visualization is not clearly different from Basic after this adjustment.



Code
task1_basic_reference <- which(task1_vistype_levels == "basic")
task1_contrast_draws <- sweep(
  task1_population_draws,
  1,
  task1_population_draws[, task1_basic_reference],
  FUN = "-"
)
task1_contrast_estimates <-
  task1_estimand_comparison$population_average -
  task1_estimand_comparison$population_average[task1_basic_reference]

# Dunnett-type simultaneous inference for the six comparisons with Basic:
# standardize each simulated contrast, take the largest absolute value across the
# six contrasts in every draw, and use its 95th percentile as the critical value.
task1_contrast_columns <- setdiff(
  seq_along(task1_vistype_levels),
  task1_basic_reference
)
task1_contrast_sd <- apply(
  task1_contrast_draws[, task1_contrast_columns, drop = FALSE],
  2,
  sd
)
task1_contrast_z_draws <- sweep(
  sweep(
    task1_contrast_draws[, task1_contrast_columns, drop = FALSE],
    2,
    colMeans(task1_contrast_draws[, task1_contrast_columns, drop = FALSE])
  ),
  2,
  task1_contrast_sd,
  FUN = "/"
)
task1_max_abs_z <- apply(abs(task1_contrast_z_draws), 1, max)
task1_dunnett_critical <- unname(quantile(task1_max_abs_z, 0.95))
task1_contrast_z <-
  task1_contrast_estimates[task1_contrast_columns] / task1_contrast_sd

task1_basic_contrasts <- tibble::tibble(
  vistype = factor(
    task1_vistype_levels[task1_contrast_columns],
    levels = task1_vistype_levels
  ),
  difference = task1_contrast_estimates[task1_contrast_columns],
  standard_error = task1_contrast_sd,
  lower_ci = difference - task1_dunnett_critical * standard_error,
  upper_ci = difference + task1_dunnett_critical * standard_error,
  p_unadjusted = 2 * pnorm(abs(task1_contrast_z), lower.tail = FALSE),
  p_adjusted = vapply(
    abs(task1_contrast_z),
    \(z) mean(task1_max_abs_z >= z),
    numeric(1)
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    vistype = factor(vistype, levels = levels(accuracy_estimates$vistype))
  )

# Text helpers: every accuracy sentence on this page is generated from the
# estimates and their intervals. A difference is described as lower or higher
# only when its interval excludes the null value (1 for odds ratios, 0 for
# differences); otherwise the text says that the data cannot distinguish it from
# no difference.
task1_format_p <- function(p) {
  formatted <- format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)
  if_else(startsWith(formatted, "<"), formatted, paste("=", formatted))
}
task1_number_words <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six")

task1_effect_sentence <- function(
  labels, estimate, lower, upper, p,
  scale = c("odds_ratio", "difference"),
  interval_text = "95% CI",
  p_text = "*p*",
  outcome = "the odds of a correct response were"
) {
  scale <- match.arg(scale)
  null_value <- if (scale == "odds_ratio") 1 else 0
  describe <- function(i) {
    if (scale == "odds_ratio") {
      sprintf(
        "%s (OR = %.2f, %s %.2f–%.2f, %s %s)",
        labels[i], estimate[i], interval_text, lower[i], upper[i],
        p_text, task1_format_p(p[i])
      )
    } else {
      sprintf(
        "%s (%+.1f pp, %s %+.1f to %+.1f pp, %s %s)",
        labels[i], 100 * estimate[i], interval_text, 100 * lower[i],
        100 * upper[i], p_text, task1_format_p(p[i])
      )
    }
  }
  lower_set <- which(upper < null_value)
  higher_set <- which(lower > null_value)
  unclear_set <- setdiff(seq_along(estimate), c(lower_set, higher_set))
  sentences <- character()
  if (length(lower_set) > 0) {
    sentences <- c(sentences, paste0(
      "Relative to Basic topoplot, ", outcome, " clearly lower for ",
      knitr::combine_words(describe(lower_set)), "."
    ))
  }
  if (length(higher_set) > 0) {
    sentences <- c(sentences, paste0(
      "Relative to Basic topoplot, ", outcome, " clearly higher for ",
      knitr::combine_words(describe(higher_set)), "."
    ))
  }
  if (length(unclear_set) == length(estimate)) {
    sentences <- c(sentences, paste0(
      "No visualization type differed clearly from Basic topoplot: all ",
      task1_number_words[length(estimate)], " intervals included ",
      null_value, "."
    ))
  } else if (length(unclear_set) > 0) {
    sentences <- c(sentences, paste0(
      "The intervals for the other ", task1_number_words[length(unclear_set)],
      " visualization type", if (length(unclear_set) > 1) "s" else "",
      " included ", null_value, "."
    ))
  }
  # Name the unclear comparisons with the lowest point estimates, so that a
  # suggestive but inconclusive difference is reported with its uncertainty.
  below_null <- unclear_set[estimate[unclear_set] < null_value]
  below_null <- below_null[order(estimate[below_null])]
  below_null <- head(below_null, 2)
  if (length(below_null) > 0) {
    sentences <- c(sentences, paste0(
      "The lowest point estimate", if (length(below_null) > 1) "s were" else " was",
      " for ", knitr::combine_words(describe(below_null)),
      ", but ", if (length(below_null) > 1) "these intervals" else "this interval",
      " also included ", null_value,
      ", so the data are compatible both with no difference and with a ",
      if (scale == "odds_ratio") "moderate reduction in the odds." else
        "moderate accuracy cost."
    ))
  }
  paste(sentences, collapse = " ")
}

title: Task 1
text:
Conditional logistic paired-choice sensitivity analysis
Task 1 is a paired-choice experiment: every trial presents one matching and one nonmatching candidate image. We therefore fitted a conditional logistic paired-choice model as a sensitivity analysis. Its candidate-image terms provide a Bradley–Terry representation of each image’s general tendency to be selected. Unlike the primary accuracy model, it assigns each of the 30 candidate images one shared attractiveness parameter regardless of whether that image is matching or nonmatching on a particular trial. It also adjusts for whether an image appeared as the second option.
The data were represented by two rows per trial, with one row for each candidate and one selected candidate within each participant–trial choice set. Visualization effects were estimated as interactions with matching-candidate status because visualization type is constant within a choice set and its main effect therefore cancels. Standard errors were clustered by participant to account for each participant’s 21 choices.


Code
task1_bt_trials <- task1 |>
  transmute(
    ID = factor(ID),
    trial,
    choice_set = interaction(ID, trial, drop = TRUE),
    vistype = relevel(factor(vistype), ref = "basic"),
    pattern = relevel(factor(pattern), ref = "MMN"),
    position_c = position - mean(position),
    stimulus = as.character(stimulus),
    correct_image = as.character(correct_image),
    wrong_image = as.character(wrong_image),
    solution,
    answered,
    recorded_correct = correct,
    opt1,
    opt2
  )

task1_bt_expected_opt1 <- if_else(
  task1_bt_trials$solution == 1L,
  task1_bt_trials$correct_image,
  task1_bt_trials$wrong_image
)
task1_bt_expected_opt2 <- if_else(
  task1_bt_trials$solution == 2L,
  task1_bt_trials$correct_image,
  task1_bt_trials$wrong_image
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(task1_bt_trials) == n_distinct(task1_bt_trials$choice_set),
  all(
    count(task1_bt_trials, ID, name = "trials")$trials == task1_n_trials
  ),
  all(task1_bt_trials$stimulus == task1_bt_trials$correct_image),
  all(task1_bt_trials$recorded_correct ==
        as.integer(task1_bt_trials$answered == task1_bt_trials$solution)),
  all(startsWith(
    basename(task1_bt_trials$opt1),
    paste0(task1_bt_expected_opt1, "_")
  )),
  all(startsWith(
    basename(task1_bt_trials$opt2),
    paste0(task1_bt_expected_opt2, "_")
  ))
)

Code
task1_bt_visual_terms <- c(
  "match_adjacent",
  "match_animation",
  "match_bivariate_corner",
  "match_bivariate_range",
  "match_triple_CI",
  "match_uncert_markers"
)
task1_bt_visual_labels <- c(
  "Adjacent plots vs Basic topoplot",
  "Animation vs Basic topoplot",
  "Bivariate corner vs Basic topoplot",
  "Bivariate range vs Basic topoplot",
  "Confidence intervals vs Basic topoplot",
  "Uncertainty markers vs Basic topoplot"
)

task1_bt_coefficients <- coef(task1_bt_fit)
task1_bt_covariance <- vcov(task1_bt_fit)
task1_bt_visual_estimates <- task1_bt_coefficients[task1_bt_visual_terms]
task1_bt_visual_standard_errors <- sqrt(
  diag(task1_bt_covariance)[task1_bt_visual_terms]
)

task1_bt_results <- tibble::tibble(
  comparison = task1_bt_visual_labels,
  estimate = unname(task1_bt_visual_estimates),
  standard_error = unname(task1_bt_visual_standard_errors)
) |>
  mutate(
    z_value = estimate / standard_error,
    p_value = 2 * pnorm(abs(z_value), lower.tail = FALSE),
    odds_ratio = exp(estimate),
    lower_ci = exp(estimate - 1.96 * standard_error),
    upper_ci = exp(estimate + 1.96 * standard_error)
  )

task1_bt_corner_result <- task1_bt_results |>
  filter(comparison == "Bivariate corner vs Basic topoplot")
task1_bt_range_result <- task1_bt_results |>
  filter(comparison == "Bivariate range vs Basic topoplot")

task1_bt_visual_covariance <- task1_bt_covariance[
  task1_bt_visual_terms,
  task1_bt_visual_terms,
  drop = FALSE
]
task1_bt_wald_chisq <- drop(
  t(task1_bt_visual_estimates) %*%
    solve(task1_bt_visual_covariance, task1_bt_visual_estimates)
)
task1_bt_wald_df <- length(task1_bt_visual_terms)
task1_bt_wald_p <- pchisq(
  task1_bt_wald_chisq,
  df = task1_bt_wald_df,
  lower.tail = FALSE
)

# Dunnett-type adjustment for the six comparisons with Basic, from the joint
# normal distribution of the participant-clustered (robust) estimates.
task1_bt_correlation <- cov2cor(task1_bt_visual_covariance)
set.seed(20261118)
task1_bt_critical <- mvtnorm::qmvnorm(
  0.95,
  tail = "both.tails",
  corr = task1_bt_correlation
)$quantile
task1_bt_results <- task1_bt_results |>
  mutate(
    lower_adjusted = exp(estimate - task1_bt_critical * standard_error),
    upper_adjusted = exp(estimate + task1_bt_critical * standard_error),
    p_adjusted = vapply(
      abs(z_value),
      \(z) 1 - as.numeric(mvtnorm::pmvnorm(
        lower = rep(-z, length(task1_bt_visual_terms)),
        upper = rep(z, length(task1_bt_visual_terms)),
        corr = task1_bt_correlation
      )),
      numeric(1)
    )
  )

task1_bt_results |>
  transmute(
    Comparison = comparison,
    `Odds ratio` = sprintf("%.2f", odds_ratio),
    `95% CI (unadjusted)` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", lower_ci, upper_ci),
    `p (unadjusted)` = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001),
    `Simultaneous 95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", lower_adjusted, upper_adjusted),
    `p (Dunnett-adjusted)` = format_pvalue_html(p_adjusted)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    escape = FALSE,
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
    caption = paste(
      "Conditional logistic paired-choice sensitivity analysis.",
      "Adjusted intervals and p values are Dunnett-type (multivariate normal)",
      "adjusted for the six comparisons with Basic, using participant-clustered",
      "standard errors. Adjusted values with p < .05 are shown in dark red."
    ),
    table.attr = kable_table_attributes
  )

model_table_note(
  paste0(
    "<ul>",
    "<li><strong>Model:</strong> Conditional logistic paired-choice model with one ",
    "stratum per participant--trial.</li>",
    "<li><strong>Bradley--Terry connection:</strong> Candidate-image effects represent ",
    "each image's shared tendency to be selected across pairings.</li>",
    "<li><strong>Image effects:</strong> One shared fixed attractiveness parameter was ",
    "estimated for each candidate image across matching and nonmatching roles.</li>",
    "<li><strong>Adjustment:</strong> Matching-candidate effects were adjusted for ERP ",
    "pattern, presentation position, and whether the candidate was shown second.</li>",
    "<li><strong>Repeated choices:</strong> Robust standard errors were clustered by ",
    "participant.</li>",
    "<li><strong>Interpretation:</strong> An odds ratio below 1 indicates weaker ",
    "preference for the matching candidate than under Basic topoplot.</li>",
    "<li><strong>Multiplicity:</strong> Both unadjusted and Dunnett-adjusted values ",
    "are shown; the joint robust Wald test is reported below.</li>",
    "</ul>"
  ),
  label = "Sensitivity-model details"
)



Sensitivity-model details:


Model: Conditional logistic paired-choice model with one stratum per participant–trial.


Bradley–Terry connection: Candidate-image effects represent each image’s shared tendency to be selected across pairings.


Image effects: One shared fixed attractiveness parameter was estimated for each candidate image across matching and nonmatching roles.


Adjustment: Matching-candidate effects were adjusted for ERP pattern, presentation position, and whether the candidate was shown second.


Repeated choices: Robust standard errors were clustered by participant.


Interpretation: An odds ratio below 1 indicates weaker preference for the matching candidate than under Basic topoplot.


Multiplicity: Both unadjusted and Dunnett-adjusted values are shown; the joint robust Wald test is reported below.











NoteTerms explanation






Conditional: The model compares the two candidate images within the same participant’s trial. It uses the fact that exactly one candidate was selected and removes the separate baseline for each trial. The term does not refer to an experimental condition.
Stratum: A stratum is one participant–trial choice set. It contains two rows: one for the matching candidate and one for the nonmatching candidate. The model compares candidates within this set, not candidates from different trials.





Sensitivity-analysis conclusion
After accounting for candidate-image attractiveness, option position, ERP pattern, and presentation position, the joint participant-clustered Wald test indicated that visualization type changed preference for the matching candidate, \(\chi^2(6) = 13.24\), p = 0.039.
Unadjusted. Relative to Basic topoplot, the odds of selecting the matching candidate were clearly lower for Bivariate range (OR = 0.68, unadjusted 95% CI 0.48–0.95, unadjusted p = 0.023). The intervals for the other five visualization types included 1. The lowest point estimates were for Bivariate corner (OR = 0.71, unadjusted 95% CI 0.50–1.00, unadjusted p = 0.051) and Uncertainty markers (OR = 0.73, unadjusted 95% CI 0.51–1.05, unadjusted p = 0.093), but these intervals also included 1, so the data are compatible both with no difference and with a moderate reduction in the odds.
Dunnett-adjusted. No visualization type differed clearly from Basic topoplot: all six intervals included 1. The lowest point estimates were for Bivariate range (OR = 0.68, simultaneous 95% CI 0.44–1.05, adjusted p = 0.1) and Bivariate corner (OR = 0.71, simultaneous 95% CI 0.45–1.11, adjusted p = 0.2), but these intervals also included 1, so the data are compatible both with no difference and with a moderate reduction in the odds.
The sensitivity analysis separates matching performance from images’ general tendency to be selected; it does not replace the primary mixed-effects accuracy analysis.

NoteDiagnostic: are the below-chance targets mis-keyed?





Question. 2 target images were matched less often than chance across all visualization types: MMN_19 (41.7%, n = 115) and MMN_29 (46.1%, n = 102). The lowest target–distractor combination with at least 10 trials was MMN_19 against N170_7 (9% correct, n = 11).
Answer key. The key is internally consistent: in all 3,129 trials, the matching candidate is the target image, its file name belongs to the target’s ERP class and to the option named by the solution code, the nonmatching file is the logged distractor, and the recorded accuracy equals “answered = solution”. There is no sign of a coding or key error.
Ambiguity, not mis-keying. The difficulty is specific to N170 distractors. When the target was an MMN image, accuracy was 56.4% against an N170 distractor and 85.9% against a P3 distractor. For the below-chance targets, accuracy against N170 distractors was 15.3% (MMN_19) and 20.5% (MMN_29), but against P3 distractors it was 69.6% (MMN_19) and 65.5% (MMN_29). As distractors, the same images were almost never chosen (94.7% correct for MMN_19 and 93.2% correct for MMN_29). Visual inspection of the stimuli (Experimental stimuli/stimuli/SE/) agrees: the MMN and N170 class templates both show a frontal negativity with a posterior positivity. These two MMN images are weak single-subject maps (colour scales of ±1.5 and ±1.7 µV) whose positivity is lateral or temporal rather than posterior, whereas several N170 images (for example N170_7, N170_12, and N170_16) closely resemble the MMN template. Participants therefore picked the image that looked more like the template, which on these trials was the distractor.
Consequence for the analysis. These trials are retained. Target and distractor random intercepts absorb image difficulty, and the trials with these targets were spread evenly over the visualization types (27–36 trials per type), so hard items add noise rather than bias.
Exploratory refit. Without the 217 trials whose target was one of these images, the likelihood-ratio test for visualization type gave p = 0.018 (all trials: p = 0.043). The two lowest odds ratios relative to Basic were Bivariate range (OR = 0.61, Dunnett-adjusted simultaneous 95% CI 0.37–1.00, adjusted p = 0.051) and Bivariate corner (OR = 0.63, Dunnett-adjusted simultaneous 95% CI 0.38–1.03, adjusted p = 0.075); all six adjusted intervals included 1. The excluded images were chosen after looking at the data, so this refit is exploratory and does not replace the primary analysis.
In the manuscript, the stimulus section should state that some single-subject MMN and N170 topographies are similar, which makes MMN–N170 pairs harder.

title: Task 1
section: Summary of the Task 1 accuracy evidence
text:
Summary of the Task 1 accuracy evidence

Overall test. Adding visualization type improved the primary model, \(\chi^2(6) =
13.03\), p = 0.043.
Primary contrasts (population-average accuracy, Dunnett-adjusted for six comparisons with Basic). No visualization type differed clearly from Basic topoplot: all six intervals included 0. The lowest point estimates were for Bivariate range (-5.1 pp, simultaneous 95% CI -11.3 to +1.1 pp, adjusted p = 0.14) and Bivariate corner (-4.5 pp, simultaneous 95% CI -10.7 to +1.7 pp, adjusted p = 0.24), but these intervals also included 0, so the data are compatible both with no difference and with a moderate accuracy cost.
Odds-ratio scale (Dunnett-adjusted). No visualization type differed clearly from Basic topoplot: all six intervals included 1. The lowest point estimates were for Bivariate range (OR = 0.67, simultaneous 95% CI 0.42–1.07, adjusted p = 0.13) and Bivariate corner (OR = 0.70, simultaneous 95% CI 0.44–1.13, adjusted p = 0.23), but these intervals also included 1, so the data are compatible both with no difference and with a moderate reduction in the odds.
Sensitivity analysis (conditional logit, Dunnett-adjusted). No visualization type differed clearly from Basic topoplot: all six intervals included 1. The lowest point estimates were for Bivariate range (OR = 0.68, simultaneous 95% CI 0.44–1.05, adjusted p = 0.1) and Bivariate corner (OR = 0.71, simultaneous 95% CI 0.45–1.11, adjusted p = 0.2), but these intervals also included 1, so the data are compatible both with no difference and with a moderate reduction in the odds.
Interpretation. Taken together, the evidence that any uncertainty visualization changed matching accuracy is weak: the overall test gave p = 0.043, and no Dunnett-adjusted contrast with Basic excluded zero. Bivariate range and Bivariate corner had the lowest estimates in both the primary model and the conditional-logit sensitivity analysis, so they are candidates for a small accuracy cost, but this study cannot distinguish that cost from no difference. The results should be reported as estimates with intervals, not as evidence that a visualization lowered accuracy.

# Country name followed by its flag (flags line up in a column at the axis).
# Flags: figures/flags/<iso2>.png from flagcdn.com, see figures/flags/SOURCES.md.
flag_tag <- function(iso, height = 11, width = 18) {
  flag_width <- if_else(!is.na(iso) & iso == "ch", height, width)
  sprintf(
    "<img src='%s' width='%d' height='%d'/>",
    project_path("figures", "flags", paste0(iso, ".png")),
    flag_width,
    height
  )
}

flag_label <- function(labels, height = 11, width = 18) {
  labels <- as.character(labels)
  display_labels <- if_else(labels == "United Kingdom", "UK", labels)
  other <- startsWith(labels, "Other")
  iso <- rep(NA_character_, length(labels))
  iso[!other] <- tolower(countrycode::countrycode(
    labels[!other], "country.name", "iso2c",
    custom_match = c(USA = "US", UK = "GB"), warn = FALSE
  ))
  dplyr::case_when(
    labels == "Other" ~ "*Other*",
    labels == "Countries at <2%" ~ "Countries at <2%",
    other ~ sub("^Other \\((.*)\\)$", "*Other*<br>(\\1)", gsub("<", "<", labels)),
    is.na(iso) ~ display_labels,
    TRUE ~ sprintf("%s %s", display_labels, flag_tag(iso, height, width))
  )
}

# Equal Earth projection (Šavrič, Patterson & Jenny, 2018): an equal-area
# pseudocylindrical projection, so country areas are not inflated toward the
# poles as in Mercator.
project_equal_earth <- function(lon, lat) {
  a1 <- 1.340264
  a2 <- -0.081106
  a3 <- 0.000893
  a4 <- 0.003796
  lambda <- lon * pi / 180
  theta <- asin(sqrt(3) / 2 * sin(lat * pi / 180))
  tibble::tibble(
    x = 2 * sqrt(3) * lambda * cos(theta) /
      (3 * (9 * a4 * theta^8 + 7 * a3 * theta^6 + 3 * a2 * theta^2 + a1)),
    y = a4 * theta^9 + a3 * theta^7 + a2 * theta^3 + a1 * theta
  )
}

Site structure

Task 1: visualization comparison.
Task 2: pattern detection.
Hit or miss: hits, near hits and misses in Task 2.

title: Quality control
text:
Two checks flag participants who may not have answered carefully. Flagged participants are kept in all main analyses; the Subjective evaluation page repeats the rating contrasts without them as a sensitivity analysis.
7 participants are flagged in total.

title: Quality control
text:
Too fast: the speed index (TIME_RSI)
SoSci Survey compares each participant’s speed with the typical participant’s (Leiner, 2019):

On each page, the median time of all participants is divided by this participant’s time. A value of 2 means “twice as fast as typical on this page”.
Any value above 3 is counted as 3, so a single page skipped in a second does not decide the result.
The page values are averaged.

As a formula, for participant \(i\):
\[
\text{TIME\_RSI}_i = \frac{1}{P} \sum_{p=1}^{P} \min\left(3,\ \frac{M_p}{t_{ip}}\right)
\]
where \(t_{ip}\) is participant \(i\)’s time on page \(p\), \(M_p\) is the median time of all participants on page \(p\), and \(P\) is the number of pages. Recomputing it this way from the page times of all 338 downloaded records reproduces SoSci’s values (correlation 1.000, mean absolute difference 0.002, i.e. rounding).
So 1 = typical speed, 2 = twice as fast. Leiner suggests treating values above 2.0 as suspicious, because such participants may not have read the questions. He also warns that speed is not a valid indicator when a questionnaire tests knowledge or skill, because experts are simply faster. Our tasks test experts’ perception, so the flag is only a hint. In this sample the median index is 1.11.
We flag values strictly above 2, as Leiner words it. One participant is exactly at 2 and is therefore not flagged (the dot on the dashed line in the figure).
Were the fast participants careless? The figure plots each participant’s speed index against their performance in both tasks.

Task 1 (two options, so guessing gives 50%): the 5 fast participants answered 67%–90% correctly (median of all participants: 76%).
Task 2 (score from 0 to 1; clicking a random region gives 0.39 on average): they scored 0.57–0.78 (median of all participants: 0.73).

All fast participants are above chance in both tasks, so they were fast but not guessing. Some of them are among the weaker participants in one task, which is why the flag is kept as a sensitivity check rather than ignored.

speed_panel <- function(y, y_label, chance, chance_label, y_labels, label_gap) {
  # ID labels go below each triangle, or above it when another flagged point sits
  # just below (otherwise the label would cover that point)
  labels <- speeders |> mutate(value = .data[[y]])
  labels$above <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(labels)), \(k) {
    others <- labels[-k, ]
    any(abs(others$time_rsi - labels$time_rsi[k]) < 0.08 &
          others$value < labels$value[k] &
          others$value > labels$value[k] - 2.5 * label_gap)
  }, logical(1))
  labels <- mutate(labels,
    label_y = if_else(above, value + label_gap, value - label_gap),
    label_vjust = if_else(above, 0, 1)
  )
  ggplot(quality_plot_data, aes(time_rsi, .data[[y]])) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = speed_cutoff, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey35") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = chance, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey35") +
    annotate("text", x = speed_cutoff + 0.03, y = Inf,
             label = sprintf("Above %s:\nflagged as too fast", speed_cutoff),
             hjust = 0, vjust = 1.1, size = 5.5, colour = "#c4501f", lineheight = 0.8) +
    annotate("text", x = 0.3, y = chance, label = chance_label,
             hjust = 0, vjust = -0.5, size = 5.5, colour = "grey25") +
    geom_point(data = filter(quality_plot_data, !speeding),
               colour = "grey70", size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_point(data = speeders, colour = "#eb6834", shape = 17, size = 5.5) +
    geom_text(data = labels, aes(y = label_y, label = ID, vjust = label_vjust),

                  y = chance - 2 * label_gap) +

title: Task 2
text:
Task 2 examined whether participants could combine information about estimated voltage and its uncertainty to locate a relevant spatial region. On each trial, participants saw one EEG topoplot and were asked to select the scalp region with the highest signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), defined as the absolute average-referenced voltage divided by its standard error. They responded using a separate scalp layout divided into 64 selectable regions.
The task included three characteristic ERP patterns: MMN, P3, and N170. Each was shown using each of the seven visualization types. This produced 21 trials per participant, each on a separate page. Trial order was randomized separately for every participant.






Figure 1: Example uncertainty-integration trial. Participants selected one of 64 regions after identifying the region with the highest SNR.

title: Task 2
text:
Response scoring and trial reconstruction

For each participan we reconstructed presentation order. Each participant went through 21 randomly shuffled pages.
For each trial, survey recorded the visualization, ERP stimulus shown and one region selected by participant. There were 64 regions on selectable grid.
The selected region was matched to the corresponding stimulus and its stored region score in regions.txt.
The region score represents |Voltage|/SE at that region. This calcaulation is actually more complicated.







NoteHow the 0–1 region score was calculated





For each stimulus, the scoring pipeline performed the following steps:

It loaded one average-referenced ERP case using the task, subject, time point, and condition recorded in task_configs_30_balanced. The fixed combinations were:



ERP pattern
Time point (index)
Condition




MMN
96
3


N170
105
2


P3
129
1



It average-referenced the voltage across the \(N\) channels:
\[
V_i^{AR} = V_i - \frac{1}{N}\sum_j V_j.
\]
It calculated a polarity-independent, t-like signal-to-noise value at each channel:
\[
T_i = \frac{|V_i^{AR}|}{SE_i}.
\]
It interpolated the channel-level \(T_i\) values into a continuous topoplot grid. Only finite interpolated cells inside the visible head mask were retained.
It fitted the saved 64-region polygon template to the topoplot domain. For each region \(k\), it averaged all retained grid cells that were inside both the polygon and the head mask:
\[
R_k = \operatorname{mean}\{T(x,y):(x,y)\in\text{region}_k\}.
\]
It min–max normalized the 64 raw region scores separately within each stimulus:
\[
S_k = \frac{R_k - \min_j R_j}{\max_j R_j - \min_j R_j}.
\]
The weakest region therefore receives 0, the strongest receives 1, and other regions are positioned proportionally between them. Scores are rounded to two decimal places.

Implementation references. The stimulus-generation source is stored under UnfoldMakie/experiments/working/:

stimulus selection: stimuli_data.jl:213;
average referencing and channel score: region_detection/rereferencing.jl:96;
topoplot interpolation: region_detection/region_score_exports.jl:48;
polygon validation and fitting: get_regions.jl:19;
regional averaging: region_detection/scoring.jl:338;
normalization, rounding, and export: region_detection/region_score_exports.jl:7.

The polygon definitions are stored in experiments/figures/task2_topo_regions_64_eeg_aligned_pipeline28/regions.jl.

title: Task 2
text:
Detection-score analysis

The primary analysis uses the extended model:
score ~ vistype + pattern + position_c +
  (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus) + (1 | stimulus:vistype)
The outcome contains exact 0 and 1 values as well as intermediate scores. An ordered-beta model retains this graded information while supporting the complete closed interval from 0 to 1. A binary logistic model would instead treat every score below 1 as equally incorrect.
Every participant completed 21 trials, so responses from the same participant are related. Adding (1 | ID) gives each participant their own baseline detection performance while estimating common visualization, pattern, and presentation-position effects.
Some stimuli may be intrinsically easier to interpret than others. Adding (1 | stimulus) gives each stimulus its own baseline score, so visualization comparisons are not attributed to stimulus difficulty alone.
Each stimulus was rendered in all seven visualizations, giving 210 distinct images, and each image was seen by about 15 participants. Adding (1 | stimulus:vistype) gives each image its own deviation from what its stimulus and visualization predict. Without it, the responses to one image would count as independent evidence about the visualization, although they share whatever made that particular image easy or hard.
ERP pattern and centered presentation position adjust the visualization comparisons for the displayed pattern and for linear change as participants progressed through the task.
The simpler base model is shown first as a reference. It contains visualization type and a participant random intercept but does not adjust for pattern, presentation position, or differences among stimuli.

  family = ordbeta(link = "logit"),

NoteWhy correlated participant-specific visualization slopes were not retained





We tested whether the effect of visualization type differed between participants by adding correlated participant-specific visualization effects: (1 + vistype | ID). The model could not estimate this full structure reliably:

It ended with convergence code 1, a non-positive-definite Hessian, and singular convergence.
The structure requires seven participant-level random coefficients and 28 variance–covariance parameters.
Each participant provided only three detection scores for each visualization type, which did not contain enough information to estimate all those parameters reliably.

We also tested simpler participant-specific structures:

A participant-specific position slope, (1 + position_c | ID), converged. Its estimated standard deviation was 0.013 on the logit scale per trial, against a fixed position effect of 0.002. Across the 20 steps from the first to the last trial, one slope SD amounts to 0.26 logit units.
A diagonal visualization structure, diag(0 + vistype | ID), which estimates separate participant-specific visualization variances without their correlations, was tried during model building. It is not refitted on this page, so no result from it is reported here.

We therefore retained participant, stimulus and image random intercepts in the primary model. This does not show that visualization effects are identical for every participant. It means that these data cannot reliably estimate the full correlated structure.

Expected detection scores

The ordered-beta model has three parts: the probability of an exact 0, the probability of an exact 1, and the mean μ of the continuous scores in between. The back-transformed estimated marginal mean from emmeans(type = "response") is μ only, so it ignores the exact 0s and 1s.
The expected score combines all three parts: E[y] = P(1) + (1 − P(0) − P(1)) μ, where P(0) and P(1) follow from the model’s two cutpoints. Because 19% of the responses are exact 1s, E[y] is noticeably higher than μ.
E[y] is reported in two forms:

Averaged over participants, stimuli and images (primary). The random intercepts are integrated out, so this is the expected score of a new participant on a new stimulus. It is directly comparable with observed means.
Typical participant, stimulus and image (random effects set to zero).

# Expected score of the ordered-beta model. glmmTMB stores the two cutpoints
# directly as the "psi" parameters: P(0) = 1 - logit^-1(eta - psi1),
# P(1) = logit^-1(eta - psi2).
task2_expected_score <- function(eta, cut_zero, cut_one) {
  p_zero <- 1 - plogis(eta - cut_zero)
  p_one <- plogis(eta - cut_one)
  p_one + (1 - p_zero - p_one) * plogis(eta)
}

task2_par_cov <- model_task2$sdr$cov.fixed
task2_is_beta <- names(task2_par) == "beta"
task2_is_theta <- names(task2_par) == "theta"
task2_is_psi <- names(task2_par) == "psi"

stopifnot(
  ncol(task2_grid_x) == sum(task2_is_beta),
  sum(task2_is_psi) == 2,
  # All random effects are scalar intercepts, so their sum is normal with the
  # summed variance.
  sum(task2_is_theta) == 3
)

# Quadrature nodes for averaging over the summed random intercepts.
task2_re_nodes <- qnorm((seq_len(201) - 0.5) / 201)

task2_expected_from_par <- function(par) {
  eta <- drop(task2_grid_x %*% par[task2_is_beta])
  cuts <- par[task2_is_psi]
  re_sd <- sqrt(sum(exp(2 * par[task2_is_theta])))
  tibble::tibble(
    vistype = task2_grid_rows$vistype,
    conditional = task2_expected_score(eta, cuts[1], cuts[2]),
    marginal = rowMeans(task2_expected_score(
      outer(eta, re_sd * task2_re_nodes, `+`),
      cuts[1],
      cuts[2]
    ))
  ) |>
    group_by(vistype) |>
    summarise(across(c(conditional, marginal), mean), .groups = "drop")
}

title: Task 2
text:
Sensitivity analysis: exact-peak responses

About 19% of responses have a score of exactly 1. Scores are rescaled within each stimulus, so a score of 1 marks the strongest region (1 stimulus has two regions tied at 1.00 after rounding to two decimals): these responses are trials in which the participant selected the strongest region. The remaining scores describe how close a miss was.
The ordered-beta model handles exact 0 and 1 values, but one linear predictor drives both the probability of a 1 and the location of intermediate scores. A visualization that helps participants find the exact peak without improving near misses (or the reverse) would therefore be averaged into a single effect.
Two checks address this:

Posterior predictive check. Data sets are simulated from the fitted ordered-beta model and compared with the observed share of exact-peak responses.
Two-part model. A logistic model for finding the exact peak and a beta model for the scores of the remaining trials, each with the same predictors and random effects as the primary model. Effects in the two parts that differ in direction or strength indicate that the single-predictor ordered-beta contrast summarizes two distinct effects.



Posterior predictive check


Code
set.seed(20261116)
task2_peak_n_sim <- 1000
task2_peak_sims <- simulate(model_task2, nsim = task2_peak_n_sim)

task2_peak_stats <- function(score, vistype) {
  per_vistype <- tibble::tibble(vistype = vistype, score = score) |>
    group_by(vistype) |>
    summarise(
      share_one = mean(score == 1),
      mean_score = mean(score),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
  basic <- per_vistype[per_vistype$vistype == "basic", ]
  per_vistype |>
    mutate(
      share_one_vs_basic = share_one - basic$share_one,
      mean_score_vs_basic = mean_score - basic$mean_score
    )
}

task2_peak_observed <- task2_peak_stats(task2_model$score, task2_model$vistype)

task2_peak_simulated <- purrr::map_dfr(
  task2_peak_sims,
  \(score) task2_peak_stats(score, task2_model$vistype),
  .id = "simulation"
)

task2_peak_ppc <- task2_peak_simulated |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    c(share_one, share_one_vs_basic, mean_score, mean_score_vs_basic),
    names_to = "statistic",
    values_to = "simulated"
  ) |>
  group_by(vistype, statistic) |>
  summarise(
    lower = quantile(simulated, 0.025),
    median = median(simulated),
    upper = quantile(simulated, 0.975),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    task2_peak_observed |>
      tidyr::pivot_longer(-vistype, names_to = "statistic", values_to = "observed"),
    by = c("vistype", "statistic")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    inside = observed >= lower & observed <= upper,

Two-part model

Exact peak: logistic mixed model for score == 1.
Closeness of misses: beta mixed model for the trials with score < 1. The 5 scores of exactly 0 were moved slightly inward with the Smithson–Verkuilen transformation, (score × (n − 1) + 0.5) / n.
Both parts use the primary model’s predictors: vistype + pattern + position_c + (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus) + (1 | stimulus:vistype).
The second part is conditional on missing the peak. If a visualization turns near misses into exact hits, its remaining misses can look worse even when overall performance improves, so the two parts should be read together.



Code
task2_peak_hit_model <- glmmTMB(
  peak ~ vistype + pattern + position_c + (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus) + (1 | stimulus:vistype),
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = mutate(task2_model, peak = as.integer(score == 1))
)

task2_peak_miss_data <- task2_model |>
  filter(score < 1) |>
  mutate(score_squeezed = (score * (n() - 1) + 0.5) / n())

task2_peak_miss_model <- glmmTMB(
  score_squeezed ~ vistype + pattern + position_c + (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus) + (1 | stimulus:vistype),
  family = beta_family(link = "logit"),
  data = task2_peak_miss_data
)

stopifnot(
  task2_peak_hit_model$fit$convergence == 0,
  isTRUE(task2_peak_hit_model$sdr$pdHess),
  task2_peak_miss_model$fit$convergence == 0,
  isTRUE(task2_peak_miss_model$sdr$pdHess)
)

      TRUE ~ "miss"
    ),
    direction = case_when(
      !excludes_zero ~ "none",
      estimate > 0 ~ "better",
      TRUE ~ "worse"
    )
  ) |>
  select(vistype, part, direction, estimate) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = part, values_from = c(direction, estimate)) |>
  rename(primary = direction_primary, peak = direction_peak, miss = direction_miss) |>
  mutate(
    pattern = case_when(
      peak == "none" & miss == "none" ~ "No clear effect in either part",
      peak != "none" & miss != "none" & peak != miss ~
        "Opposite effects on exact peak and misses",
      peak != "none" & miss != "none" ~ "Same effect in both parts",
      peak != "none" ~ paste0(
        "Exact peak only (", if_else(peak == "better", "more", "fewer"), " exact hits)"
      ),
      TRUE ~ paste0(
        "Misses only (", if_else(miss == "better", "closer", "farther"), " misses)"
      )
    ),
    primary_captures = case_when(
      primary == "none" & (peak != "none" | miss != "none") ~
        "No: the ordered-beta contrast shows no clear effect",
      primary != "none" & peak != "none" & peak != primary ~
        "Partly: the exact-peak effect has the opposite direction",
      primary != "none" &
        sign(estimate_peak) != sign(estimate_primary) ~
        "Partly: the exact-peak estimate points the other way (interval includes zero)",
      primary != "none" &
        sign(estimate_miss) != sign(estimate_primary) ~
        "Partly: the miss estimate points the other way (interval includes zero)",
      TRUE ~ "Yes"
    )
  )

title: Task 2
section: Sensitivity analysis: rank and top-3 outcomes
text:
Sensitivity analysis: rank and top-3 outcomes


Code
# Rank of every region within its stimulus by score (1 = strongest region).
task2_region_ranks <- region_scores |>
  group_by(stimulus) |>
  mutate(
    rank_average = rank(-score, ties.method = "average"),
    rank_min = rank(-score, ties.method = "min"),
    n_regions = n()
  ) |>
  ungroup()

task2_tenth_best <- task2_region_ranks |>
  filter(rank_min == 10)

# task2_model keeps the row order of task2 (no rows are dropped, checked above),
# so the selected region can be attached by position.
stopifnot(identical(as.character(task2_model$stimulus), as.character(task2$stimulus)))

task2_rank_model_data <- task2_model |>
  mutate(region = task2$region) |>
  left_join(
    task2_region_ranks |> select(stimulus, region, rank_average, rank_min, n_regions),
    by = c("stimulus", "region")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # 1 = strongest region, 0 = weakest; ties share their average rank.
    rank_score = (n_regions - rank_average) / (n_regions - 1),
    top3 = as.integer(rank_min <= 3)
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(task2_rank_model_data) == nrow(task2_model),
  !anyNA(task2_rank_model_data$rank_score)
)

# Most frequently selected region for each stimulus and its rank by score.
task2_modal_regions <- task2_rank_model_data |>
  count(pattern, stimulus, region, rank_min, score, name = "responses") |>
  group_by(stimulus) |>
  slice_max(responses, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

task2_p3_low_modal <- task2_modal_regions |>
  filter(pattern == "P3", rank_min > 3)
task2_p3_low_modal_top_region <- names(which.max(table(task2_p3_low_modal$region)))
task2_p3_low_modal_top_region_n <- max(table(task2_p3_low_modal$region))
task2_p3_low_modal_top_ranks <- task2_p3_low_modal |>
  filter(region == task2_p3_low_modal_top_region) |>
  pull(rank_min)



Why a sensitivity analysis. Region values are min–max rescaled within each stimulus, so the same score does not mean the same thing for different stimuli. For example, the 10th-strongest region has a score between 0.24 and 0.90, depending on the stimulus. Score magnitudes, and differences between them, should therefore not be compared across stimuli. The visualization comparisons are within stimuli (every stimulus is shown in every visualization), but the score scale still weights a miss differently for different stimuli.
Two outcomes that do not depend on the score scale.

Rank score: the rank of the selected region among the 64 regions of its stimulus, mapped to 0–1 (1 = strongest region, 0 = weakest; tied regions share their average rank). Modelled with the same ordered-beta model as the primary analysis.
Top 3: whether the selected region is among the three strongest regions of its stimulus (39% of responses). Modelled with a logistic mixed model.
Both models use the primary predictors and random effects: vistype + pattern + position_c + (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus) + (1 | stimulus:vistype).




Code
task2_rank_model <- glmmTMB(
  rank_score ~ vistype + pattern + position_c +
    (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus) + (1 | stimulus:vistype),
  family = ordbeta(link = "logit"),
  data = task2_rank_model_data
)

task2_top3_model <- glmmTMB(
  top3 ~ vistype + pattern + position_c +
    (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus) + (1 | stimulus:vistype),
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = task2_rank_model_data
)

stopifnot(
  task2_rank_model$fit$convergence == 0,
  isTRUE(task2_rank_model$sdr$pdHess),
  task2_top3_model$fit$convergence == 0,
  isTRUE(task2_top3_model$sdr$pdHess)
)

task2_outcome_contrasts <- list(
  `Score (primary)` = model_task2,
  `Rank score` = task2_rank_model,
  `Top 3` = task2_top3_model
) |>
  purrr::imap_dfr(\(model, name) {
    set.seed(20261118)
    emmeans(model, ~vistype, at = list(position_c = 0)) |>
      contrast(method = "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = "basic", adjust = "mvt") |>
      as.data.frame() |>
      transmute(
        outcome = name,
        vistype = stringr::str_remove(contrast, " - basic$"),
        estimate,
        SE,
        p.value
      )
  }) |>
  mutate(
    outcome = factor(outcome, levels = unique(outcome)),
    vistype = factor(vistype, levels = levels(task2_model$vistype))
  )

task2_outcome_contrasts |>
  arrange(vistype) |>
  transmute(
    vistype = table_vistype(vistype),
    outcome,
    value = if_else(
      p.value < 0.05,
      sprintf(
        '<span style="color:#B2182B;font-weight:700">%+.2f (p = %s)</span>',
        estimate, sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p.value))
      ),
      sprintf("%+.2f (p = %s)", estimate, sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p.value)))
    )
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = value) |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    escape = FALSE,
    col.names = c("Visualization vs Basic topoplot", levels(task2_outcome_contrasts$outcome)),

      "Differences from Basic topoplot on the logit scale for the primary score and the",
      "two scale-free outcomes, with Dunnett-adjusted p values (six comparisons within",
      "each outcome). Adjusted p < .05 is shown in dark red."

    paste0(
      paste(

Open question about the scoring. For 4 of 10 P3 stimuli, the most frequently selected region was R25, which ranks only 10th–14th by score for those stimuli. Participants may have targeted the voltage peak rather than the SNR peak. If so, low scores on these stimuli partly reflect how participants understood the task, not only how well a visualization conveyed uncertainty. This is a construct-validity question for the scoring and is not resolved here.

title: Task 2
text:
Completion-time analysis
Completion time is analysed on the Time analysis page.

title: Time analysis
text: Completion time for both tasks: how long participants spent on each trial page, by visualization type, and (for Task 1) how time relates to accuracy.

title: Time analysis
text:
Outlier rule
One rule applies to every table, figure, and model on this page: a trial page time above 180 s (3 minutes) is excluded.

Why a fixed cap. Each trial is one decision on one page. The median page time is 12 s (Task 1) and 13 s (Task 2), so a page open for more than three minutes (over ten times the median) most likely records an interruption, not time spent on the task. The longest pages lasted 5,264 s and 11,221 s. The cap is fixed in seconds rather than estimated from the data, so it does not depend on which visualizations are slow.
What it removes. Task 1: 19 of 3,129 trials (0.6%, from 11 participants). Task 2: 21 of 3,129 trials (0.7%, from 15 participants).
What it replaces. Earlier versions of this page dropped trials outside 1.5 × IQR within each visualization for the descriptive tables only, while the models kept every trial. That rule removed 259 (Task 1, 8.3%) and 230 (Task 2, 7.4%) trials, mostly ordinary slow trials. The cap was chosen after the time distributions had been seen, so both alternatives are reported as sensitivity analyses below.

What the model estimates are. The models analyze log time. Back-transformed estimates are geometric mean times for a typical participant (participant effect at zero) at the average presentation position. They are not arithmetic mean times, which are larger because time is right-skewed. Differences from Basic topoplot are reported as ratios of geometric means: a ratio of 1.40 means 40% longer.
Multiple comparisons. The primary comparisons are the six visualizations against Basic topoplot within each task, with Dunnett-adjusted 95% confidence intervals and p values (emmeans dunnettx). The same family is used on the Task 1, Task 2 and rating pages.

title: Time analysis
text:
Task 1: comparison

SoSci Survey records the time spent on each questionnaire page. Each Task 1 trial has its own page (pages 5–25 hold trials 1–21), and a page keeps its number when the display order is randomized. TIME005–TIME025 are therefore the times of trials 1–21. Each time is linked to its trial, and the presentation position is taken from the logged display order.
The check below plots time by presentation position. With a correct link, the first trial a participant sees is the slowest, and times then fall as participants learn the task.







NoteCheck: completion time by presentation position

Data: Trial pages of at most 180 s (outlier rule at the top of the page).

# Plain-language descriptions follow the confidence intervals, so the text stays
# correct when the data change.
describe_association <- function(lower, upper, null, more, less, none) {
  dplyr::case_when(lower > null ~ more, upper < null ~ less, TRUE ~ none)
}

describe_time_accuracy <- function(correlation_table, effects) {
  c(
    correlation = describe_association(
      correlation_table$lower_ci,
      correlation_table$upper_ci,
      0,
      "participants who were generally slower were more accurate",
      "participants who were generally slower were less accurate",
      "participants' typical speed was not clearly associated with their accuracy"
    ),
    within = describe_association(
      effects$lower_ci[1],
      effects$upper_ci[1],
      1,
      "a participant's slower trials were more often answered correctly",
      "a participant's slower trials were less often answered correctly",
      "a participant's slower trials were not clearly more or less accurate"
    ),
    between = describe_association(
      effects$lower_ci[2],
      effects$upper_ci[2],
      1,
      "after adjustment, generally slower participants were more accurate",
      "after adjustment, generally slower participants were less accurate",
      "after adjustment, generally slower participants were not clearly more or less accurate"
    )
  )
}

task1_time_accuracy_text <- describe_time_accuracy(
  task1_time_accuracy_correlation_table,
  task1_time_accuracy_effects
)


At the participant level, accuracy and typical completion time had a Pearson correlation of 0.105 (95% CI -0.057 to 0.262, p = 0.202). In the adjusted mixed model, doubling the time spent on a trial was associated with an odds ratio of 0.745 for a correct response (95% CI 0.660 to 0.842). The between-participant odds ratio was 1.195 (95% CI 0.988 to 1.445).
In short, participants’ typical speed was not clearly associated with their accuracy; a participant’s slower trials were less often answered correctly; and after adjustment, generally slower participants were not clearly more or less accurate. These are associations, not effects of time: a harder trial can both take longer and be answered incorrectly more often.

title: Time analysis
text:
Task 2: detection

SoSci Survey records the time spent on each questionnaire page. Each Task 2 trial has its own page (pages 29–49 hold trials 1–21), and a page keeps its number when the display order is randomized. TIME029–TIME049 are therefore the times of trials 1–21. Each time is linked to its trial, and the presentation position is taken from the order variables (A207).
The check below plots time by presentation position. With a correct link, the first trial a participant sees is the slowest, and times then fall as participants learn the task.
Only non-missing positive times with an identified visualization type and at most 180 s are retained (outlier rule). The same trials enter the descriptive table and the model.
The model analyzes log completion time because trial times are positive and typically right-skewed:
log(time_sec) ~ vistype + position_c + (1 | ID)
The participant random intercept allows participants to have different typical response speeds. Presentation position adjusts for linear changes in speed across the 21 trials. Back-transformed estimates are geometric mean times for a typical participant.

title: Open-ended feedback
text:
Participants included in the qualitative content analysis: 69.
Meaning units extracted: 274 unique units, coded to visualizations in 288 rows. 12 units evaluate more than one visualization (for example, one statement that several named plots were easy to interpret) and therefore appear once per visualization they evaluate.
Participant comments are presented in two groups. Select an Expand button to read the responses.

title: Open-ended feedback
text:
Qualitative content analysis
ID links every unit to its original A305 response. Participant wording is retained as closely as possible; themes and intensities are interpretive codes. Use the search box or column filters to explore the table.
References to bivariate plots without an identified variant are coded as General bivariates; a unit is coded to both Bivariate corner and Bivariate range only when the response names both variants (IDs 74 and 102). Proposed redesigns are included only when they express an evaluation of the displayed visualization; suggestions alone are not assigned an intensity.






WarningCoding is not yet validated



The units were coded by large language models with one fixed prompt (data/a305_content_analysis_prompt.md): GPT-5.6 Sol (via Codex) coded the first responses and Claude coded the responses of later participants (IDs 115 and above) and checked all codes against the coding rules. No human coder has checked the codes yet, so the themes and intensities below are provisional. A random subsample is prepared for a human second coder (see Inter-coder agreement).
The coders used the neutral code 0 for only 3 of 274 units, so the intensity scale is in practice a four-point negative/positive scale.


Download the content analysis as an Excel workbook

Theme codebook





Theme
Explanation




Accessibility
Usability across color vision, devices, or other viewer needs.


Aesthetics
Visual attractiveness, cleanliness, or perceived ugliness.


Information integration
How well multiple quantities are combined without obscuring one another.


Informativeness
Amount or usefulness of information communicated.


Interpretability
Ease or difficulty of understanding what the visualization means.


Learnability
Whether interpretation becomes easier with exposure or practice.


Legend/color mapping
Clarity and intuitiveness of colors, scales, and their legends.


Medium compatibility
Suitability for print, papers, presentations, screens, or animation.


Preference
An explicit choice, ranking, liking, or dislike.


Reading effort
Time, attention, or cognitive effort required to extract information.


SNR visibility
How clearly signal-to-noise ratio or uncertainty can be identified.


Space/scalability
Figure size, visual density, or ability to accommodate multiple plots.


Task suitability
Usefulness for a particular analytical or comparison task.

title: Open-ended feedback
section: Evaluation intensity by theme and visualization type
text:
Evaluation intensity by theme and visualization type
This descriptive analysis gives each participant at most one value within each visualization–theme combination. It therefore avoids treating multiple meaning units from the same participant as independent observations. Comments coded as General bivariates are retained in the original dataset but excluded here because they do not identify one of the seven visualization types.
A unit that evaluates several visualizations (12 units) counts once in each of those visualizations, because it is an evaluation of each, but it is never counted twice within one visualization. Comparisons across visualizations are therefore not independent where a participant evaluated several visualizations in one statement.
Cells with only one or two participants are shown as faded points without a box in the figure, and without a median or mean in the table. They are too sparse to summarise.
